title: Improving Quantum Error Correction By Meshing Surface Code With IBM’s Heavy-Hex Architecture
gist: Quantum Elements and USC researchers published a Nature paper showing the surface code error-correction scheme can be successfully mapped onto IBM's heavy-hex qubit lattice despite the topology mismatch, using Quantum Elements' Orbit error-suppression tool inside IBM's Qiskit Functions Catalog — a result that decouples fault-tolerant QPU design from having to physically match the surface-code grid.

themes.theme: Quantum Elements' business model and product

insights.claim: Quantum Elements is a three-year-old startup (as of 2026) that builds AI-based digital twins for simulating and modeling quantum computing systems, via its Constellation platform, which combines AI agents, natural-language interfaces, and simulation tools for creating/testing quantum software, generating code, and building digital twins of quantum systems.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: A quantum-software/simulation tooling vendor positioning itself as infrastructure for the pre-fault-tolerant quantum era; watch for partnerships with hardware vendors (IBM) as a monetization path.
insights.locator: Quantum Elements is a three-year-old startup

insights.claim: Quantum Elements co-founder and CEO Izhar Medalsy has compared the need for quantum digital-twin simulation to established EDA tools, saying organizations need to simulate quantum systems the way Cadence, Ansys, or Synopsys simulate transistors, in order to virtualize large-scale quantum processors and predict how the next generation will look.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Frames quantum digital-twin/simulation software as an analog to the semiconductor EDA market — a potentially large, sticky tooling category if quantum computing scales, worth tracking for comparable-company analysis.
insights.quote: you need the ability to look at the system in the same way that flow simulators are simulating the flow of air on the wing of an airplane, or in the same way that Cadence and Ansys or Synopsis are simulating transistors in order to be able to virtualize those huge GPUs and CPUs and be able to predict how the next generation is going to look.
insights.locator: As Izhar Medalsy, co-founder and chief executive officer

insights.claim: In July 2026, Quantum Elements launched Orbit, a quantum error-suppression tool, and made it available through IBM's Qiskit Functions Catalog, a platform of pre-built, managed cloud software services for quantum research.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Signals a commercial distribution channel: third-party quantum software vendors can monetize through IBM's managed Qiskit marketplace rather than needing direct enterprise sales.
insights.locator: In July, Quantum Elements introduced Orbit

insights.claim: Quantum Elements markets Orbit as letting researchers, developers and enterprise quantum teams improve quantum circuit performance while reducing the time, cost, and workflow friction typically associated with error mitigation and suppression, without requiring deep specialization and without added processing overhead or extended compile time.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Vendor claim of an accessibility/cost advantage for error suppression — a potential wedge product for enterprises without dedicated quantum-error-correction expertise.
insights.quote: researchers, developers and enterprise quantum teams a new way to improve quantum circuit performance while reducing the time, cost and workflow friction often associated with error mitigation and suppression methods
insights.locator: The release of Orbit in Qiskit gives

themes.theme: The Nature paper: surface code on mismatched hardware

insights.claim: Researchers from Quantum Elements and the University of Southern California published a paper this month (September 2026) in Nature showing that the surface code — a topological quantum error-correction code laid out on a 2D grid and considered one of the most practical routes to large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing — can still scale error correction when run on a QPU whose physical qubit layout doesn't share that grid topology.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Removes a hardware-design constraint for fault-tolerant quantum computing: chipmakers no longer need to physically match qubit layout to the surface-code grid to get its error-correction benefits.
insights.locator: In a paper published this month in Nature

insights.claim: The research specifically applied the surface code to IBM's Heron quantum processor, which uses a heavy-hex (hexagonal/honeycomb) qubit lattice architecture rather than the square grid the surface code natively assumes.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Ties an academic breakthrough directly to IBM's specific commercial hardware line, making it relevant to IBM's own fault-tolerant quantum roadmap.
insights.locator: The research used the surface code with the heavy-hex architecture

insights.claim: IBM's Heron quantum processor, first released in 2023, comes in 133-qubit and 156-qubit configurations and is used in IBM's System Two and upgraded System One quantum systems.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Concrete hardware specs for IBM's current-generation commercial quantum processor line, useful for benchmarking against competitors' qubit counts.
insights.locator: The research used the surface code with the heavy-hex architecture of IBM’s Heron

insights.claim: IBM's heavy-hex architecture arranges qubits on a hexagonal lattice specifically to prevent crowded connections and reduce collisions between neighboring qubits.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Explains IBM's core hardware design rationale, which the new research shows does not have to sacrifice compatibility with the leading error-correction code.
insights.locator: The heavy-hex architecture is a qubit layout

insights.claim: Quantum Elements CEO Izhar Medalsy said the hybrid surface-code-on-mismatched-hardware research "shows the power of hybrid approaches to move us towards fault tolerant quantum computing," and that running hybrid code on QPUs for error correction gives engineers more design freedom instead of being locked into matching a chip's physical layout to the code.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Reframes fault-tolerant quantum computing progress as coming from software/hybrid techniques as much as from hardware topology choices — a bullish signal for software-layer quantum vendors, not just chipmakers.
insights.quote: shows the power of hybrid approaches to move us towards fault tolerant quantum computing
insights.locator: Quantum Elements’ Medalsy said in a statement

themes.theme: Technical mechanisms enabling the mismatch fix

insights.claim: The paper's authors state that implementing the surface code on QPUs with different fixed connectivities is a problem of both fundamental and practical importance, because QPU design is often driven by considerations other than optimal surface-code performance, such as avoiding frequency crowding that affects crosstalk and gate performance, and reducing circuit-element density to ease thermal management in lithographic fabrication.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Identifies the real engineering trade-offs (crosstalk, thermal management, fabrication density) that force hardware architectures away from the surface code's ideal grid — explaining why this compatibility research matters commercially, not just academically.
insights.quote: Implementing the surface code on other QPUs with different fixed connectivities is a problem of both fundamental interest and practical importance
insights.locator: the researchers wrote in their paper

insights.claim: The key technical challenge was reduced connectivity between the surface code's grid and the heavy-hex layout, which could cause delays in state transfer between non-neighboring qubits and increased exposure to decoherence-inducing noise during idle times, meaning errors could grow as the code scales up; mapping the surface code onto IBM's architecture also required additional routing.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Pinpoints the specific failure mode (idle-time noise exposure, added routing) that any team attempting cross-topology error correction must solve.
insights.locator: A key challenge was overcoming the reduced connectivity

insights.claim: To make the mismatch work, the researchers used a depth-efficient error-correction code (reducing the number of sequential gate/measurement layers that cause idle-time noise), combined with dynamical decoupling — delivered via Quantum Elements' Orbit Qiskit function — and SWAP-based embedding (using SWAP gates to exchange qubit states) to map logical qubits onto the physical Heron hardware.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Gives the concrete technical recipe (depth-efficient codes + dynamical decoupling + SWAP-based embedding) that other teams could replicate on different mismatched hardware, and shows Orbit playing a load-bearing role in a peer-reviewed result.
insights.locator: They also used the dynamical decoupling

insights.claim: This combination of techniques produced 'directional subthreshold scaling,' described as a key step in error correction that increases the code's size in a particular direction while reducing a corresponding type of error.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: A specific, named technical result (directional subthreshold scaling) that investors/technologists tracking quantum error-correction progress can use as a benchmark term to search for follow-on research.
insights.locator: This led to directional subthreshold scaling

insights.claim: IBM announced heavy-hex as the foundational topology for all of its quantum devices roughly five years before this 2026 research (i.e., around 2021), and IBM researchers had at the time laid out reasoning for the architecture in a lengthy report that also discussed the surface code as an example of contemporary error-correction-code development work.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: This new research validates a multi-year-old IBM hardware architecture bet, suggesting IBM's quantum roadmap decisions from ~2021 are now bearing out in peer-reviewed error-correction results.
insights.locator: Successfully using the surface code with IBM’s heavy-hex architecture

insights.claim: IBM's own researchers had argued that other lattice connectivities, such as the square lattice the surface code natively wants, can be simulated on the heavy-hex lattice with constant overhead by introducing SWAP operations within a suitably chosen unit cell, mapping virtual-lattice nearest-neighbor gates onto heavy-hex vertices via additional two-qubit gates, at a cost that is negligible compared to encoding costs.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: IBM had already theorized the mathematical mechanism (constant-overhead SWAP-based simulation of square-lattice connectivity) years before this research empirically confirmed it works on real hardware.
insights.quote: The connectivity of other lattices, such as the square lattice, can be simulated on the heavy-hex lattice with constant overhead by introducing swap operations within a suitably chosen unit cell.
insights.locator: IBM researchers laid out their reasoning
